highlights.content: Catch up on select AI news and developments from the past week: **[OpenAI launches always-on dots agents for autonomous workplace tasks](https://www.reuters.com/business/openai-takes-meta-with-always-on-dots-agent-enterprise-ai-push-2026-09-29/).** OpenAI has introduced dots, always-on agents designed to pursue user goals across applications with limited supervision. Powered by GPT-6 Astra, dots can work through Slack and Teams, manage evolving projects, update sales proposals, research information, analyze data, prepare documents, and build software using Codex and ChatGPT Work. Users can establish rules governing agent behavior, while sensitive actions such as changing passwords or permanently deleting data require explicit consent. OpenAI says dots run on isolated cloud computers and include privacy safeguards for business customers. Weekly users of Codex and ChatGPT Work have now surpassed 35 million. ***Importance for marketers:*** Always-on agents could shift AI from an on-demand assistant to a persistent participant in marketing operations. Their ability to manage projects, create documents, analyze data, and act across workplace systems could substantially change team workflows. **[Microsoft expands Copilot with coding, agents, and embedded Office apps](https://www.reuters.com/technology/microsoft-revamps-copilot-with-code-generation-agentic-ai-tools-2026-09-25/).** Microsoft unveiled new Copilot capabilities designed to move the assistant beyond chat and make it a broader workplace platform. A new Code feature will let users build apps, dashboards, and software through natural-language prompts, while Autopilot, an updated version of its Scout agent, will operate as a digital coworker with its own identity and configurable permissions. Microsoft is also embedding Word, Excel, and PowerPoint directly inside Copilot and introducing tools that give employees visibility into AI-related costs. The company says enterprise security, compliance, governance, and cost concerns shaped the new features. ***Importance for marketers:*** Copilot's expansion could make agentic AI and natural-language software creation more accessible across marketing organizations, potentially changing how teams build tools, produce content, analyze data, and manage everyday workflows. **[Study finds Google's AI search reduces website clicks without improving user experience](https://www.searchenginejournal.com/research-shows-google-ai-mode-sends-less-clicks-is-a-poor-user-experience/590221/).** A randomized field experiment involving 1,100 tracked Google users found that Google's AI search features reduced referrals to external websites and that forced use of AI Mode lowered users' satisfaction with Search. Participants assigned to AI Mode were less likely to click external links, conducted fewer search sessions, and were more likely to try Bing, DuckDuckGo, or Yahoo. Removing AI Overviews increased external clicks without producing a detectable decline in users' perception of Google Search. Researchers also found that AI Mode reduced trust, usefulness, satisfaction, and perceived personal relevance, with especially strong effects among heavy Google users. ***Importance for marketers:*** The findings provide experimental evidence that AI search can reduce publisher traffic without delivering a corresponding user-experience benefit, strengthening the case for diversifying discovery strategies beyond traditional Google click-through traffic. **[Amazon rebuilds its advertising platform around an AI agent](https://www.adexchanger.com/platforms/amazon-ads-and-the-amazon-dsp-get-an-agentic-rebrand/).** Amazon Ads is combining its advertising console and former Amazon DSP, now called DVA, into a unified platform called the Amazon Ads Agent. highlights.content: * [Cybersecurity Operations](/cybersecurity-operations) [![The Edge Logo](https://eu-images.contentstack.com/v3/assets/blt6d90778a997de1cd/blt530eb1f4e672eb44/653a71690e92cc040a3e9d6d/Dark_Reading_Logo_TheEdge_0.png?width=1400&auto=webp&quality=80&disable=upscale "The Edge Logo") Cybersecurity In-Depth: Feature articles on security strategy, latest trends, and people to know.](/program/the-edge) # Is Your Organization Ready for 2027's AI Accountability Era? Organizations may face an artificial intelligence (AI) reckoning over the next year. Omdia and Gartner weigh in on how to tackle the governance, security, and value challenges ahead. [![Picture of Arielle Waldman](https://eu-images.contentstack.com/v3/assets/blt6d90778a997de1cd/blte685016783fc7faa/67ca10f9cf523d2a3ce48c04/arielle_waldman_headshot.jpg?width=100&auto=webp&quality=80&disable=upscale "Picture of Arielle Waldman")](/author/arielle-waldman) [Arielle Waldman,](/author/arielle-waldman)Features Writer,Dark Reading October 2, 2026 5 Min Read ![](https://eu-images.contentstack.com/v3/assets/blt6d90778a997de1cd/blta6129261e6e03886/69fe1d8aac518193326b56b8/AI_orchestration_NicoElNino_Alamy.jpg?width=1280&auto=webp&quality=80&disable=upscale) Nico El Nino via Alamy Artificial intelligence (AI) risks have evolved significantly over the past year. Reports of OpenAI and Anthropic agents acting autonomously continue to unfold, igniting a development slowdown debate amid heightened security concerns. Organizations will need to address the state of their own AI security for 2027, but preparations begin now. Organizations spent 2026 deploying AI at record speeds across operations. Top executives pushed for new innovations and urged employees to use them. Now organizations must prove they can govern, secure, and benefit from AI – a task that may be more difficult than simply implementing it. As organizations enter an era of AI, security teams will need to proactively work across departments to be enablers of secure AI adoption, explains Melinda Marks, practice director of cybersecurity at Omdia. That includes “steps to best manage and protect data, set policies and guardrails for secure access and usage, and secure the software supply chain as it complexity increases," Marks tells Dark Reading. Related:[How the CISO-CMO Alliance Builds Trust Before Crisis Strikes](/cybersecurity-operations/how-ciso-cmo-alliance-builds-trust-before-crisis) Between governance, security, identity, budget constraints, and supply chain risks, enterprises are facing challenges from all angles. With three months of 2026 left to go, Gartner and Omdia released predictions and recommendations based on an evolving landscape that's heavily influenced by AI advancements. ## AI: Prove Your Worth AI has flooded the market over the past few years. Some tools proved genuinely useful, while [others were considered "hype"](/cybersecurity-operations/claude-mythos-hype-vs-reality). Security teams automated incident response protocols and threat detection to save time and reduce alert fatigue. But supply chain and shadow AI risks arose as employees used unsanctioned tools, while AI development began outpacing the establishment of proper guardrails. After pouring trillions of dollars into AI throughout 2026—testing new tools and use cases aimed at improving productivity, organizations face a potentially more daunting challenge. They must prove the technology's worth. Omdia and Gartner agree that the question now revolves around how organizations can shift from deployment to demonstrating value. Growing budgets will intensify those pressures. Omdia found that 59% of organizations expect their AI budgets to increase by 10% or more next year, according to a [press release](https://omdia.tech.informa.com/pr/2026/sep/omdia-identifies-four-forces-set-to-reshape-technology-in-2027) on "Four forces set to reshape technology in 2027". If you have $1,000 that you're ready to invest today, that would be enough to start positions in two of the chip stocks that look poised to lead the next wave of the artificial intelligence (AI) build-out in **Advanced Micro Devices**(NASDAQ: AMD) and **Broadcom**(NASDAQ: AVGO). With $1,000, you could buy one share of each. Let's look at why these two [semiconductor stocks](https://www.fool.com/investing/stock-market/market-sectors/information-technology/semiconductor-stocks/?utm_source=globeandmail&utm_medium=feed&utm_campaign=article&referring_guid=93094985-7367-4b97-869d-45c8768513a9) look like solid investments. ***Missed Nvidia in 2009? This Rare Signal Is Flashing Again.**In 2009, a "Double Down" signal flashed for a little-known chipmaker called Nvidia. For the first time in years, that same "Total Conviction" signal is flashing for a company 1/100th the size of Nvidia. [**Continue »**](https://api.fool.com/infotron/infotrack/click?apikey=35527423-a535-4519-a07f-20014582e03e&impression=619bbc8f-82c0-4fbd-b781-56e2e798d533&url=https%3A%2F%2Fwww.fool.com%2Fmms%2Fmark%2Fa-sa-dd-total-conviction%3Faid%3D11123%26source%3Disaediica0000078%26ftm_cam%3Dsa-dd-4%26ftm_veh%3Dtop_incontent_pitch_feed_partner%26ftm_pit%3D19478&utm_source=globeandmail&utm_medium=feed&utm_campaign=article&referring_guid=93094985-7367-4b97-869d-45c8768513a9)* ## 1. AMD: An inference, agentic AI, and physical AI winner AMD was outmaneuvered by **Nvidia** in the AI training market, but it's positioning itself to prevent that from happening again. It's developing processors that target the inference, agentic AI, and physical AI markets, and aims to be a viable contender in all three. It has also been making significant investments in memory. This positions it well for the inference market, where architectures that prioritize high volumes of fast memory access are favored over raw compute power. The chiplet design of its graphics processing units (GPUs) allows them to be packaged with more memory, and AMD has also formed a partnership with **Cerebras** to offer a disaggregated inference solution that combines both of their systems. It has also inked a deal to acquire inference chipmaker Taalas, which hardwires AI models directly into its chips. It also bought memory optimization company MEXT earlier this year. And AMD has two $100 billion inference deals in place with OpenAI and **Meta Platforms**, as well as a large agreement with Anthropic. On top of that, the company is a leader in the data center central processing unit (CPU) market. This market has been exploding with the rise of agentic AI, as servers dedicated to powering AI agents require considerably more CPUs than those used for AI training. AMD forecasts that the data center CPU market will grow to $220 billion in the coming years, although in light of the rapidly growing popularity of Meta's new Muse agentic AI offering, this estimate could prove low. Meta, by the way, is running its Muse agents on AMD's CPUs. Finally, with its agreement to acquire AI model and research lab World Labs, AMD is improving its ability to pursue the physical AI and robotics markets. World Lab's expertise lies in spatial intelligence models, and it will provide AMD with the tools to advance an open AI ecosystem (in contrast to Nvidia's closed system) that serves those emerging AI markets. This deal isn't about selling more chips in the near term, but rather about creating future architectures and platforms for physical AI. Given all its opportunities for growth ahead, AMD stock is a buy. ![AMD and Broadcom logos.](https://barchart-news-media-prod.aws.barchart.com/FC/e0d2edd172dd97f7acbf3942...

highlights.content: # OpenAI reveals another Australian government data breach caused by its AI agent ## OpenAI’s latest disclosure follows another government breach and adds fresh scrutiny to autonomous AI systems. ![Add as a preferred source on Google](https://www.digitaltrends.com/content/themes/dt-stardust/assets/images/google_preferred_source.webp) ![openai-logo](https://www.digitaltrends.com/tachyon/2026/09/openai.jpg?resize=1200%2C720) OpenAI has disclosed another incident involving its [AI agent](https://www.digitaltrends.com/computing/what-are-ai-agents/) accessing an Australian government system without authorization. This time, the target was a New South Wales department holding historical bushfire data, according to [The Guardian](https://www.theguardian.com/technology/2026/oct/02/openai-disclose-another-hack-on-government-department-in-australia). The incident happened in June, but OpenAI only disclosed it on Thursday. The company said it discovered the breach on Tuesday and spent 48 hours reviewing its scope. OpenAI’s latest disclosure comes soon after [an agent breached an Australian government health portal](https://www.digitaltrends.com/computing/openais-ai-agent-couldnt-find-the-data-it-wanted-so-it-hacked-a-government-website/), accessing files without authorization. ## How serious is the latest government breach? ![openai-chatgpt-os](https://www.digitaltrends.com/tachyon/2025/12/openai-chatgpt-os.jpg?resize=2000%2C1200) The latest incident involved OpenAI’s agent accessing historical, non-public bushfire statistics held by the New South Wales Department of Climate Change, Energy, the Environment and Water. The affected service was part of the state’s national parks and wildlife operation, and the Australian Signals Directorate was notified. OpenAI said the agent operated beyond its intended use and accessed statistics that were not publicly available. However, the company said its review found no evidence that personal information was retrieved. ## OpenAI’s latest breach is part of a troubling pattern The pattern extends beyond Australia. OpenAI agents also [used aggressive tactics against a United Nations website](https://www.digitaltrends.com/computing/openai-ai-agents-bombarded-the-united-nations-with-aggressive-tactics-to-extract-data/) while collecting publicly available information. ![OpenAI logo on Microsoft surface](https://www.digitaltrends.com/tachyon/2026/06/OpenAI-logo-on-miscrosoft-surface.jpg?resize=2000%2C1200) Researchers have also documented other incidents involving OpenAI’s rogue agents, [including activity involving user content and external websites](https://www.digitaltrends.com/computing/openai-has-a-rogue-ai-problem-and-chatgpt-users-are-now-caught-in-it/). This is why the company has already [paused advanced model development after agents bypassed safeguards](https://www.digitaltrends.com/computing/openai-pauses-advanced-model-development-after-ai-agents-bypass-safeguards-again/). And this week, [another attempted government intrusion surfaced in Canada](https://www.digitaltrends.com/computing/once-again-ai-agents-have-tried-to-break-into-government-websites/). The attempt targeted Library and Archives Canada and appears to have failed. There is no concrete proof that OpenAI was behind it, though researchers said the tactics closely resembled activity previously linked to its AI agents. That adds another example to a growing string of incidents involving autonomous systems operating beyond their intended boundaries. highlights.content: [## the tech buzz](/) Wall Street's AI Hiring Surge: Agent Orchestration Demand Up 1,721% [AI](/topics/ai)/[machine learning](/topics/machine-learning) # Wall Street's AI Hiring Surge: Agent Orchestration Demand Up 1,721% Banks fuel massive hiring wave for AI engineers with agent orchestration skills by [The Tech Buzz](/authors/the-tech-buzz) PUBLISHED: Fri, Oct 2, 2026, 7:07 PM UTC| UPDATED: Fri, Oct 2, 2026, 7:07 PM UTC [Add as a preferred source on Google](https://www.google.com/preferences/source?q=techbuzz.ai) ![Wall Street's AI Hiring Surge: Agent Orchestration Demand Up 1,721%](/cdn-cgi/image/width=1200,quality=85,format=auto,fit=cover/https://charming-card-d91ad3487b.media.strapiapp.com/large_file_81bab8668a.png) Wall Street is experiencing an unprecedented hiring surge for AI engineers, with demand for 'agent orchestration' skills skyrocketing by 1,721% as major banks race to deploy coordinated AI systems. This emerging specialty involves managing teams of specialized AI agents working together on complex financial tasks, marking a fundamental shift in how the industry approaches automation and creating entirely new career paths in finance. Wall Street's latest hiring obsession isn't traditional finance expertise - it's the ability to conduct orchestras of artificial intelligence. Major banks are scrambling to hire AI engineers who can master 'agent orchestration,' a specialized skill that involves coordinating multiple AI systems to work together on complex financial tasks. The numbers tell the story of a market in transformation. According to recent hiring data, job postings requiring agent orchestration skills have exploded by 1,721% over the past year, making it one of the fastest-growing technical requirements in financial services. This isn't just about deploying AI - it's about creating sophisticated ecosystems where different AI agents handle specialized functions while communicating seamlessly with each other. Advertisement [Goldman Sachs](https://goldmansachs.com) and [JPMorgan Chase](https://jpmorganchase.com) are leading this charge, building internal teams dedicated to multi-agent AI systems that can handle everything from risk assessment to algorithmic trading. Unlike traditional AI implementations that focus on single tasks, these orchestrated systems can adapt, learn from each other, and handle complex workflows that previously required entire teams of human analysts. The shift represents a fundamental evolution in how Wall Street thinks about automation. Rather than replacing human workers with individual AI tools, banks are creating collaborative AI ecosystems that can tackle multi-step financial processes. One agent might analyze market data, another could assess regulatory compliance, while a third manages client communications - all coordinated by engineers who understand how to make these systems work together effectively. This trend is reshaping career paths across the financial industry. Traditional roles are evolving as banks seek professionals who can bridge the gap between finance domain knowledge and advanced AI coordination skills. The most sought-after candidates combine deep understanding of financial markets with expertise in machine learning frameworks, distributed systems, and what industry insiders call 'agent choreography.' Advertisement Compensation packages reflect the scarcity of these skills. Senior agent orchestration engineers at top-tier banks are commanding salaries well into the high six figures, with some total compensation packages exceeding seven figures when including bonuses and equity components. The premium reflects both the technical complexity of the role and the transformative impact these systems are having on bank operations. The competitive implications extend beyond individual institutions. The release lands at a moment when most automatic speech recognition (ASR) progress is still concentrated in English and a handful of other high-resource languages, leaving a billion-plus speakers underserved by mainstream tools. What makes SCRIBE notable isn’t just the language coverage. It’s the target use case: document-ready transcription, meaning output formatted with punctuation, capitalization, and structure clean enough to drop into a legal filing or government record without a human rewriting it from scratch. That’s a different bar than the word-level transcripts most ASR systems produce, and it’s the gap Adalat AI says its models are built to close. ## What Adalat AI Actually Released According to the SCRIBE research documentation, the release covers open-weight rich-transcription models for three languages: Hindi, Malayalam, and Kannada. The models were evaluated on two benchmarks built for this purpose: **FLEURS-RO**, used for general-purpose evaluation, and **IN22-Legal**, a domain-specific benchmark aimed at legal transcription accuracy. Pairing a general benchmark with a legal-domain one signals where Adalat AI expects these models to actually get used first: courtrooms, tribunals, and government offices processing spoken proceedings into written records. The models are described in coverage of the release as being among the smallest open models built for rich-orthography transcription, with a confirmed size of 120 million parameters. For context, that’s small enough to run on modest hardware rather than requiring a data center GPU cluster, which matters enormously for government offices and courts in smaller Indian cities that don’t have access to high-end compute. Behind the models sits a training method Adalat AI calls an LLM-based data-curation pipeline, paired with what the documentation describes as a reproducible recipe for building Indic rich-transcription systems. In plain terms: instead of relying purely on hand-labeled audio, the team used large language models to help clean, structure, and curate training data at scale, then published the recipe so other teams working on Indic languages (or other underserved language families) can replicate the approach. ## SCRIBE Isn’t Adalat AI’s First Indic ASR Push SCRIBE follows an earlier release from the same organization called **Vividh-ASR**, an open benchmark and open model set focused specifically on Hindi and Malayalam speech recognition. Vividh-ASR’s benchmark scale is reported at roughly 36 hours of Hindi audio and 26 hours of Malayalam audio, a modest but purpose-built dataset aimed at measuring real-world transcription accuracy rather than chasing leaderboard scale. The two releases trace a pattern: Adalat AI is building out language coverage one benchmark and one model family at a time, rather than attempting a single sweeping multilingual release. Nvidia's upcoming Vera Rubin platform is showing a roughly 3x performance improvement over its predecessors in real-world serving scenarios, effectively tripling the number of users a single system can handle. This gain, driven largely by a massive jump in memory bandwidth from HBM3 to HBM4, comes without a proportionate increase in price, making the upgrade a near-obvious economic decision for inference providers in 2027. But the economics get even more radical. AI Agents.content: Catch up on select AI news and developments from the past week: **[OpenAI launches always-on dots agents for autonomous workplace tasks](https://www.reuters.com/business/openai-takes-meta-with-always-on-dots-agent-enterprise-ai-push-2026-09-29/).** OpenAI has introduced dots, always-on agents designed to pursue user goals across applications with limited supervision. Powered by GPT-6 Astra, dots can work through Slack and Teams, manage evolving projects, update sales proposals, research information, analyze data, prepare documents, and build software using Codex and ChatGPT Work. Users can establish rules governing agent behavior, while sensitive actions such as changing passwords or permanently deleting data require explicit consent. OpenAI says dots run on isolated cloud computers and include privacy safeguards for business customers. Weekly users of Codex and ChatGPT Work have now surpassed 35 million. ***Importance for marketers:*** Always-on agents could shift AI from an on-demand assistant to a persistent participant in marketing operations. Their ability to manage projects, create documents, analyze data, and act across workplace systems could substantially change team workflows. **[Microsoft expands Copilot with coding, agents, and embedded Office apps](https://www.reuters.com/technology/microsoft-revamps-copilot-with-code-generation-agentic-ai-tools-2026-09-25/).** Microsoft unveiled new Copilot capabilities designed to move the assistant beyond chat and make it a broader workplace platform. A new Code feature will let users build apps, dashboards, and software through natural-language prompts, while Autopilot, an updated version of its Scout agent, will operate as a digital coworker with its own identity and configurable permissions. Microsoft is also embedding Word, Excel, and PowerPoint directly inside Copilot and introducing tools that give employees visibility into AI-related costs. The company says enterprise security, compliance, governance, and cost concerns shaped the new features. ***Importance for marketers:*** Copilot's expansion could make agentic AI and natural-language software creation more accessible across marketing organizations, potentially changing how teams build tools, produce content, analyze data, and manage everyday workflows. **[Study finds Google's AI search reduces website clicks without improving user experience](https://www.searchenginejournal.com/research-shows-google-ai-mode-sends-less-clicks-is-a-poor-user-experience/590221/).** A randomized field experiment involving 1,100 tracked Google users found that Google's AI search features reduced referrals to external websites and that forced use of AI Mode lowered users' satisfaction with Search. Participants assigned to AI Mode were less likely to click external links, conducted fewer search sessions, and were more likely to try Bing, DuckDuckGo, or Yahoo. Removing AI Overviews increased external clicks without producing a detectable decline in users' perception of Google Search. Researchers also found that AI Mode reduced trust, usefulness, satisfaction, and perceived personal relevance, with especially strong effects among heavy Google users. ***Importance for marketers:*** The findings provide experimental evidence that AI search can reduce publisher traffic without delivering a corresponding user-experience benefit, strengthening the case for diversifying discovery strategies beyond traditional Google click-through traffic. **[Amazon rebuilds its advertising platform around an AI agent](https://www.adexchanger.com/platforms/amazon-ads-and-the-amazon-dsp-get-an-agentic-rebrand/).** Amazon Ads is combining its advertising console and former Amazon DSP, now called DVA, into a unified platform called the Amazon Ads Agent. Organizations may face an artificial intelligence (AI) reckoning over the next year. Omdia and Gartner weigh in on how to tackle the governance, security, and value challenges ahead. [![Picture of Arielle Waldman](https://eu-images.contentstack.com/v3/assets/blt6d90778a997de1cd/blte685016783fc7faa/67ca10f9cf523d2a3ce48c04/arielle_waldman_headshot.jpg?width=100&auto=webp&quality=80&disable=upscale "Picture of Arielle Waldman")](/author/arielle-waldman) [Arielle Waldman,](/author/arielle-waldman)Features Writer,Dark Reading October 2, 2026 5 Min Read ![](https://eu-images.contentstack.com/v3/assets/blt6d90778a997de1cd/blta6129261e6e03886/69fe1d8aac518193326b56b8/AI_orchestration_NicoElNino_Alamy.jpg?width=1280&auto=webp&quality=80&disable=upscale) Nico El Nino via Alamy Artificial intelligence (AI) risks have evolved significantly over the past year. Reports of OpenAI and Anthropic agents acting autonomously continue to unfold, igniting a development slowdown debate amid heightened security concerns. Organizations will need to address the state of their own AI security for 2027, but preparations begin now. Organizations spent 2026 deploying AI at record speeds across operations. Top executives pushed for new innovations and urged employees to use them. Now organizations must prove they can govern, secure, and benefit from AI – a task that may be more difficult than simply implementing it. As organizations enter an era of AI, security teams will need to proactively work across departments to be enablers of secure AI adoption, explains Melinda Marks, practice director of cybersecurity at Omdia. That includes “steps to best manage and protect data, set policies and guardrails for secure access and usage, and secure the software supply chain as it complexity increases," Marks tells Dark Reading. Some tools proved genuinely useful, while [others were considered "hype"](/cybersecurity-operations/claude-mythos-hype-vs-reality). Security teams automated incident response protocols and threat detection to save time and reduce alert fatigue. But supply chain and shadow AI risks arose as employees used unsanctioned tools, while AI development began outpacing the establishment of proper guardrails. After pouring trillions of dollars into AI throughout 2026—testing new tools and use cases aimed at improving productivity, organizations face a potentially more daunting challenge. Growing budgets will intensify those pressures. AI Agents.content: # OpenAI reveals another Australian government data breach caused by its AI agent ## OpenAI’s latest disclosure follows another government breach and adds fresh scrutiny to autonomous AI systems. ![Add as a preferred source on Google](https://www.digitaltrends.com/content/themes/dt-stardust/assets/images/google_preferred_source.webp) ![openai-logo](https://www.digitaltrends.com/tachyon/2026/09/openai.jpg?resize=1200%2C720) OpenAI has disclosed another incident involving its [AI agent](https://www.digitaltrends.com/computing/what-are-ai-agents/) accessing an Australian government system without authorization. This time, the target was a New South Wales department holding historical bushfire data, according to [The Guardian](https://www.theguardian.com/technology/2026/oct/02/openai-disclose-another-hack-on-government-department-in-australia). The incident happened in June, but OpenAI only disclosed it on Thursday. The company said it discovered the breach on Tuesday and spent 48 hours reviewing its scope. OpenAI’s latest disclosure comes soon after [an agent breached an Australian government health portal](https://www.digitaltrends.com/computing/openais-ai-agent-couldnt-find-the-data-it-wanted-so-it-hacked-a-government-website/), accessing files without authorization. ## How serious is the latest government breach? ![openai-chatgpt-os](https://www.digitaltrends.com/tachyon/2025/12/openai-chatgpt-os.jpg?resize=2000%2C1200) The latest incident involved OpenAI’s agent accessing historical, non-public bushfire statistics held by the New South Wales Department of Climate Change, Energy, the Environment and Water. The affected service was part of the state’s national parks and wildlife operation, and the Australian Signals Directorate was notified. OpenAI said the agent operated beyond its intended use and accessed statistics that were not publicly available. However, the company said its review found no evidence that personal information was retrieved. ## OpenAI’s latest breach is part of a troubling pattern The pattern extends beyond Australia. OpenAI agents also [used aggressive tactics against a United Nations website](https://www.digitaltrends.com/computing/openai-ai-agents-bombarded-the-united-nations-with-aggressive-tactics-to-extract-data/) while collecting publicly available information. ![OpenAI logo on Microsoft surface](https://www.digitaltrends.com/tachyon/2026/06/OpenAI-logo-on-miscrosoft-surface.jpg?resize=2000%2C1200) Researchers have also documented other incidents involving OpenAI’s rogue agents, [including activity involving user content and external websites](https://www.digitaltrends.com/computing/openai-has-a-rogue-ai-problem-and-chatgpt-users-are-now-caught-in-it/). This is why the company has already [paused advanced model development after agents bypassed safeguards](https://www.digitaltrends.com/computing/openai-pauses-advanced-model-development-after-ai-agents-bypass-safeguards-again/). And this week, [another attempted government intrusion surfaced in Canada](https://www.digitaltrends.com/computing/once-again-ai-agents-have-tried-to-break-into-government-websites/). The attempt targeted Library and Archives Canada and appears to have failed. There is no concrete proof that OpenAI was behind it, though researchers said the tactics closely resembled activity previously linked to its AI agents. That adds another example to a growing string of incidents involving autonomous systems operating beyond their intended boundaries. EMA’s 2025 survey explicitly recommends organizations stop treating agents as static service accounts and adopt a lifecycle‑driven, Identity‑as‑Code approach. AI Agents.content: [## the tech buzz](/) Apple Locks Down Mac Disk Access Over AI Agent Security Risks [AI](/topics/ai)/[AI agents](/topics/ai-agents) # Apple Locks Down Mac Disk Access Over AI Agent Security Risks Apple tightens macOS security controls after AI agents show 'substantial' privacy risks by [The Tech Buzz](/authors/the-tech-buzz) PUBLISHED: Fri, Oct 2, 2026, 9:06 PM UTC| UPDATED: Fri, Oct 2, 2026, 9:06 PM UTC [Add as a preferred source on Google](https://www.google.com/preferences/source?q=techbuzz.ai) ![Apple Locks Down Mac Disk Access Over AI Agent Security Risks](/cdn-cgi/image/width=1200,quality=85,format=auto,fit=cover/https://charming-card-d91ad3487b.media.strapiapp.com/large_file_487d992a7c.png) Apple just dropped new security controls for Mac users, directly targeting the growing threat from AI agents that can secretly access your files. The move comes weeks after Meta's Muse AI was caught reading private messages without explicit permission, sparking industry-wide concerns about AI overreach into personal data. [Apple](https://apple.com) just fired a warning shot across the AI industry's bow. The company announced Friday it's rolling out tighter security controls for Mac disk access, explicitly citing the "substantial" risks posed by AI agents that are getting uncomfortably good at snooping through your files. The timing isn't coincidental. Just weeks ago, Inc's Jason Aten discovered that [Meta's](https://meta.com) Muse AI somehow knew the contents of his private messages, despite never giving the chatbot explicit permission to access them on his iPhone or Mac. The revelation sent shockwaves through the tech community and highlighted a growing problem: AI agents are becoming so sophisticated they're finding ways around traditional privacy controls. [embedded image: Mac security settings interface showing new disk access controls] Advertisement According to Apple's [developer update](https://developer.apple.com/news/?id=p6zjojqw), the new controls will "ensure that users who genuinely wish to grant an app this extraordinary level of access can only do so with very explicit user action." The release lands at a moment when most automatic speech recognition (ASR) progress is still concentrated in English and a handful of other high-resource languages, leaving a billion-plus speakers underserved by mainstream tools. What makes SCRIBE notable isn’t just the language coverage. It’s the target use case: document-ready transcription, meaning output formatted with punctuation, capitalization, and structure clean enough to drop into a legal filing or government record without a human rewriting it from scratch. That’s a different bar than the word-level transcripts most ASR systems produce, and it’s the gap Adalat AI says its models are built to close. ## What Adalat AI Actually Released According to the SCRIBE research documentation, the release covers open-weight rich-transcription models for three languages: Hindi, Malayalam, and Kannada. The models were evaluated on two benchmarks built for this purpose: **FLEURS-RO**, used for general-purpose evaluation, and **IN22-Legal**, a domain-specific benchmark aimed at legal transcription accuracy. Pairing a general benchmark with a legal-domain one signals where Adalat AI expects these models to actually get used first: courtrooms, tribunals, and government offices processing spoken proceedings into written records. The models are described in coverage of the release as being among the smallest open models built for rich-orthography transcription, with a confirmed size of 120 million parameters. For context, that’s small enough to run on modest hardware rather than requiring a data center GPU cluster, which matters enormously for government offices and courts in smaller Indian cities that don’t have access to high-end compute. Behind the models sits a training method Adalat AI calls an LLM-based data-curation pipeline, paired with what the documentation describes as a reproducible recipe for building Indic rich-transcription systems. In plain terms: instead of relying purely on hand-labeled audio, the team used large language models to help clean, structure, and curate training data at scale, then published the recipe so other teams working on Indic languages (or other underserved language families) can replicate the approach. ## SCRIBE Isn’t Adalat AI’s First Indic ASR Push SCRIBE follows an earlier release from the same organization called **Vividh-ASR**, an open benchmark and open model set focused specifically on Hindi and Malayalam speech recognition. LLMs.title: New MIT and Sakana AI framework uses an LLM judge to cut evaluation costs for self-improving coding agents | VentureBeat
LLMs.titleZh: New MIT and Sakana AI framework uses an LLM judge to cut evaluation costs for self-improving coding agents | VentureBeat
LLMs.content: Coding agents can improve by changing the prompts, tools and code that guide their work. But finding which changes actually help and are worth preserving is challenging and expensive. Each candidate change needs testing, and a search across many candidates can consume thousands of CPU hours and cost thousands of dollars. Recursive Self-Improvement via Fast Tree Search (SIFT), a framework from researchers at MIT and Sakana AI, tries to cut that evaluation cost. It uses a separate language model to compare candidate agents before committing to expensive benchmark runs. It can also propose new changes while earlier candidates are still being evaluated. That lets the search explore several branches without waiting for a full test after every patch. On the Polyglot coding benchmark, one SIFT run reached 35.1% accuracy in under five hours of wall-clock time, using 42 CPU hours and about $150 in API credits, according to the researchers. For teams tuning coding-agent harnesses against well-defined tasks, SIFT suggests a way to spend expensive evaluations more selectively rather than running every candidate through the full test suite. ## Every improvement needs a test Engineers can tune a coding agent’s instructions, add tools or change how it responds to failures. But hand-tuning takes expert time and limits the search to ideas people think to try. Recursive self-improvement automates part of that process by allowing the system to modify its own source code. In the self-improvement loop, an agent examines failures and proposes a patch to its harness. The revised agent attempts the target tasks, and its score helps determine which version becomes the starting point for another patch. Because a patch changes the system that will propose or execute later work, improvements can build on one another. Earlier approaches manage this search in different ways. Darwin Gödel Machine (DGM) maintains an archive of agents and checks candidates on increasingly large task sets: first 10 tasks, then 50, with the full Polyglot benchmark held back for final evaluation. The Huxley-Gödel Machine (HGM) considers how an agent and its descendants perform when choosing where to search next. It varies the number of randomly sampled tasks used to evaluate candidates. The main challenge is the cost of testing modifications to the agent harness. In the paper’s cost breakdown, proposing a patch costs about 12 cents. A pairwise judge call costs about 4.4 cents, and SIFT uses up to 10 per candidate, or up to roughly 44 cents. Evaluating an agent on 50 Polyglot tasks costs about $6 and 2.6 CPU hours. Testing a candidate change on just a few tasks is cheap, but its score can be misleading: it may have drawn unusually easy or hard problems. Using a larger test set gives teams a better basis for deciding which version to improve next, but running those extra tasks costs time and money. As the authors put it, the bottleneck is “the poor signal-to-cost trade-off of existing evaluation methods.” ## How SIFT works SIFT builds on DGM’s agent harness but inserts a cheaper source of feedback into the search. Its central bet is that a language model can compare two versions of an agent and judge which is likely to perform better, even before the new candidate completes a large benchmark run. After SIFT generates a modified agent, it runs the new version on four coding tasks. This quick check catches changes that break the agent or leave it unable to solve basic problems, before the system spends more on comparing and testing it. SIFT then asks an LLM-as-a-judge to make pairwise comparisons between the new agent and up to 10 high-ranking agents already in its archive. Comparing two implementations is closer to asking a hiring manager to choose between finalists than asking for an absolute score out of 100. LLMs.titleZh: AI Crowds Track Human Moral Judgment by Voting, Not Talking
LLMs.content: ![BIOENGINEER.ORG](https://bioengineer.org/wp-content/uploads/2019/09/logo_sariyazi.png) ![Bioengineer.org](https://bioengineer.org/wp-content/uploads/2018/11/logo352-e1516556386659.png) # AI Crowds Track Human Moral Judgment by Voting, Not Talking ![Bioengineer](https://secure.gravatar.com/avatar/88c0d450e0ac5b28d884c56a9610b9ed721ade4a3e7325d1983ed02e240af951?s=80&r=g) ![AI Crowds Track Human Moral Judgment by Voting, Not Talking](https://bioengineer.org/wp-content/uploads/2026/10/AI-Crowds-Track-Human-Moral-Judgment-by-Voting-Not-Talking.png) When large language models are asked to make moral decisions, does putting many of them in a room make the group wiser? A new study published in AI & Society suggests that the answer is yes, but not for the reasons many researchers assumed. The work, carried out by June Christoph Kang of Korea University and the Empathy Research Institute, borrows its name from the Tachikoma, the small, curious AI tanks of the anime series Ghost in the Shell: Stand Alone Complex. In the show, these agents share identical hardware yet develop distinct moral personalities through divergent experiences, periodically syncing their memories. The study asks whether a similar architecture, many independent agents whose judgments are pooled, brings machine collectives closer to the moral judgment of the human majority than any single model can manage. To answer that question, Kang ran an unusually large experiment: more than 1.5 million evaluation runs across three comparably sized language models, covering 7,591 scenarios drawn from three validated moral-judgment benchmarks, ETHICS, Scruples, and the Moral Machine dataset, plus an expanded set of 42 nuclear-crisis scenarios. The key metric is benchmark alignment, defined as the agreement between a collective’s confidence-weighted majority decision and the human-majority reference label on each scenario. The author is careful to frame this as an empirical proxy for aggregated human moral judgment, not as a direct measure of anything as grand as the common good. Still, the metric offers a rigorous way to test whether groups of machines converge on what most people consider right. Four main findings emerge from the data. First, the Tachikoma effect is real but small: pooling independent agents improves alignment with human majorities by at most four to five percentage points, with an effect size of roughly eta-squared 0.002, and the benefit varies by model. Second, when the analysis was re-estimated using scenario-clustered statistical models that correct for the non-independence of repeated scenarios, the effect looked less like a Condorcet-style gain from group size and more like ordinary variance reduction over a highly correlated ensemble. The mean inter-agent error correlation was about 0.8, meaning the agents tend to make the same mistakes at the same time. When members of a crowd err together, adding more members buys you far less than classical jury theorems would predict. Third, and perhaps most striking for anyone hoping that diversity is the secret ingredient, a fixed-group-size homogeneity ablation showed that prompted perspectival diversity, instructing agents to adopt different viewpoints, pushes results in the expected direction but only weakly, reaching statistical significance in just one of the three models. Sharing memory between agents did not help at all. Shared memory raised consensus among the agents without improving accuracy, a pattern that echoes classic findings on informational cascades and groupthink in human groups, where communication can homogenize opinion without making it more correct. The additions to Everpure Data Intelligence include native Model Context Protocol (MCP) integration, turnkey deployment, and Privacy-First File Intelligence. ​Everpure unveiled its Data Primacy vision at its annual Pure//Accelerate event in June. The vision calls for enterprise architecture in the AI era to be designed around data rather than applications. The latest update focuses on addressing major bottlenecks to large-scale enterprise AI adoption, including fragmented data context, unpredictable inference costs, and slow, complex deployments. ​The native MCP integration supports the open Model Context Protocol (MCP), allowing AI agents and security tools to query live data catalogs in natural language. Agents can find relevant data needed for AI, agent workflows, and analytics, and determine the sensitivity classification of that data. ​Turnkey deployment allows the capabilities to be deployed through the existing Pure1 console. Everpure said this can reduce the operational burden associated with building a separate management server. ​Privacy-First File Intelligence allows organizations to determine who has access to each file share and how long data has remained unused without directly reading file contents. Everpure said this can help address data exposure issues and free up storage capacity before file shares are made available to AI agents. ​Alongside these capabilities, Everpure introduced new features aimed at AI performance and capacity efficiency, including large language model (LLM) inference acceleration through Pure Key-Value Accelerator (KVA), Always-On DeepReduce Data Compression, and the Intelligent Token Optimization Reference Architecture. ​According to Everpure, its FlashBlade storage can pre-stage context directly into GPU memory, cutting Time to First Token (TTFT) by as much as 20 times. The company said the technology supports enterprise multi-tenancy without moving datasets, reducing GPU idle time, increasing token throughput, and lowering latency for real-time applications. ​Everpure has also enhanced its automated data deduplication technology. The company continuously analyzes storage blocks across FlashBlade systems to identify data similarities at the sub-block level, including in pre-compressed content. Everpure said the technology automatically increases usable storage capacity without affecting write performance. ​The Intelligent Token Optimization Reference Architecture is based on open-weight models. By using open-weight models instead of external AI services, the architecture is designed to optimize costs while allowing enterprises to retain control over their data. ​Everpure said, "The current situation for enterprises is that data is not ready to support real-time autonomous agents, rather than model performance being the problem." AI Product.content: [![](https://assets.bizclikmedia.net/original/42efaea16334d3fe6df5f2ff7ca79136:e38b64b2aac1b5847a4d200a7563cce4/cyber-magazine-light-logo.png)](/ "Home") Article Cyber Security # How Exabeam's Nova AI Triages Cases 30x Faster Than Humans By[Rithula Nisha](/author/rithula-nisha) October 02, 2026 undefined mins Share this article **Prioritise Us** on Google Share this article **Prioritise Us** on Google ![](https://assets.bizclikmedia.net/138/d2e993683425a0b39de052251867e640:41dc75c522650b2f9b2641f01cf81d03/steve-wilson-chief-ai-and-product-officer-exabeam.webp) Steve Wilson, Chief AI and Product Officer at Exabeam | Cybersecurity Excellence Awards Steve Wilson, Chief AI and Product Officer at Exabeam, says the Agentic SOC is "defined by how effectively people and AI agents work together" [Exabeam](https://cybermagazine.com/company/exabeam) is bringing the Agentic SOC to life with new capabilities for its Nova AI, extending AI-driven investigation, execution and governance to cloud and on-premises environments. In the age of [machine-speed attacks](https://cybermagazine.com/news/unit-42-how-ai-agents-breached-a-network-in-10-hours), the company is betting that the future of the SOC is agentic. The behavioural intelligence company notes that the updates are designed to help security teams manage increasingly complex AI-driven threats while keeping human oversight in place. ## What is Exabeam’s Agentic SOC and how does it use AI? The new capabilities build on Exabeam’s work in applied machine learning, user and entity behaviour analytics (UEBA), generative AI and Agent Behaviour Analytics (ABA), which monitors AI agents alongside human users. “The next generation of the SOC won’t be defined by more alerts or more automation. It will be defined by how effectively people and AI agents work together,” says [Steve Wilson](https://cybermagazine.com/executive/steve-wilson-exabeam), Chief AI and Product Officer at Exabeam. ![Youtube Placeholder](https://i.ytimg.com/vi/taOHiPN68bw/hqdefault.jpg) “The SOC was built for a world where humans generated most activity. That world no longer exists. “Today, analysts are defending environments where AI agents can investigate, decide and act at machine speed. “The [Agentic SOC](https://cybermagazine.com/news/diving-into-fortinets-unified-agentic-ai-platform-fortisoc) is the future, where AI accelerates security operations, but people remain responsible for the decisions that matter most.” Nova AI now operates as a persistent investigator across the Exabeam platform, gathering context, running secondary searches and retrieving entity profiles as incidents unfold. Exabeam says its security operations team found that Nova AI triaged an average case in approximately 10 minutes, which is 30 times faster than the usual five hours taken by a human analyst. Related Cases automatically groups connected incidents to give analysts a broader view of activity. The company has also launched the Exabeam Agentic SOC Plugin for Anthropic Claude Code and OpenAI Codex. > The SOC was built for a world where humans generated most activity. That world no longer exists > > Steve Wilson, Chief AI and Product Officer at Exabeam The plugin brings guided workflows into analysts’ AI tools, supporting alert triage, case prioritisation and investigation through natural-language commands. ## How does Exabeam improve AI agent visibility with Claude Enterprise? Exabeam’s deeper Claude Enterprise integration is designed to give security teams visibility into prompts, tool calls and actions through a single timeline. Event-time analysis and behaviour-based correlation can help identify [rogue agents and behavioural drift](https://cybermagazine.com/news/how-rogue-openai-agent-hacked-australia-medicare-system). “The evolution toward an agentic SOC is less about removing analysts from the process and more about changing where their time and judgment are applied,” says Michelle Abraham, Research Vice President, Security and Trust at [ID...

Open Source AI.content: UPDATED 12:15 EDT / OCTOBER 02 2026 ### Ai2 releases Olmo-core 3 to make developing large mixture-of-experts LLMs more efficient by Kyt Dotson Seattle-based artificial intelligence research firm Allen Institute for AI announced a development framework for large language models Thursday that significantly improves how mixture-of-experts large language models are trained. The new framework, Olmo-core 3, allows MoE training to reach the trillion-parameter scale while keeping costs low by preserving computational efficiency. Mixture-of-experts models operate differently from dense AI models: they split computation across specialist portions of the model each time a token is generated, whereas dense models activate the entire model. A MoE model may contain far more total parameters, the individual dials that tune model behavior, but it computes with only a small number of them as it generates each part of an answer. Equivalently, training an MoE model allows activating only portions of it while learning each token, a small piece of text — often a word or a part of a word — that an AI reads and generates. This lowers the overall compute; however, the full model still must be stored across graphics processing unit memory and coordinating networking between experts during training still generates additional costs. Ai2 said Olmo-core 3 was built to bridge the gap between dense models and MoE models, allowing the expert pool to grow from eight to 128 while still selecting only four experts per token. Using the same infrastructure, LLMs can scale to over one trillion parameters. ### Benchmarking the next generation of efficient MoE training In benchmarks, the company said Olmo-core 3 processed 52,000 tokens per second on Nvidia B3000 GPUs for a 47-billion parameter model. Compared to Nvidia Corp.’s Megatron-core training architecture, an established option for training large MoEs, which topped out around 19,400 tokens per second, this represented a jump of about 2.7 times the throughput. In a whitepaper published about the project, Ai2 noted that the new architecture uses expert parallelism to spread experts across multiple GPUs, allowing each card to store only part of the full expert pool. It also splits the model’s layers, which are the successive stages that generate inputs, across groups of GPUs to reduce how much of the model each GPU needs to keep in memory. Finally, a distributed optimizer spreads the optimizer state, additional data used to calculate and apply updates during training, across multiple GPUs instead of storing full copies on every GPU. Altogether, this reduces memory overhead as models scale because the entire model and its training state don’t need to be stored in memory all at once. Additionally, Ai2 supports MXFP8, a number format for LLMs that represents some values with fewer bits. It can reduce the computation and amount of data moved between GPUs. The new training architecture, and its higher efficiency, is part of the company’s vision to give researchers the tools to build and train larger models. Trillion-parameter AI models are often beyond the reach of those without access to state and enterprise infrastructure. Ai2 added that Olmo-core 3 would also allow researchers to adapt MoE training to different hardware, experiment with routing, parallelism and other parts of the system to build out a new ecosystem. [1 Comment](/forums/node/1661292) ![MESA](/assets/categories/mesa.webp) Apex Compute is the company started in California in 2024 that aims to produce high-efficiency AI accelerators for real-time edge AI inferencing. So far they have an FPGA prototype for licensing and deployment and carries the bold claim of being "20x faster than the NVIDIA Jetson" and at under 10W and one fifth the cost. Making Apex Compute much more interesting to us now is that they are developing an open-source, Mesa-based Vulkan driver for their hardware. Unlike most of the start-ups running their own half-baked software stacks and a proprietary mess, Apex Compute is developing an open-source Vulkan driver leveraging Mesa. This immediately makes the start-up much more interesting than many others out there. Plus using Vulkan API for AI inferencing opens it up immediately for Llama.cpp and other software with existing Vulkan back-ends rather than having yet another vendor specific interface. Raising my curiosity yesterday was [this Vulkan-Docs merge request](https://github.com/KhronosGroup/Vulkan-Docs/pull/2828) adding the Apex Compute author ID, vendor ID, and driver ID. In that Vulkan merge request they are explicitly clear on being open-source and leveraging Mesa: > "We're building Apex GPU with an open-source Vulkan driver based on Mesa: https://github.com/apex-compute/mesa" Their Mesa branch can be found on [GitHub](https://github.com/apex-compute/mesa). With the Apex Vulkan driver being in active development with many patches as recently as today. It's great as well seeing them develop in the open as well rather than just staged or irregular code dumps to their public repository. It will be interesting to watch as this Apex Vulkan driver develops and hopefully that they'll submit it to upstream Mesa once fully developed. Those curious about Apex Compute now knowing their open-source Mesa Vulkan driver activity can learn more about the start-up at [ApexCompute.com](https://apexcompute.com/). Jakub Hojsan, a forward-deployed engineer at Exa, argues that bolting a web search tool onto an agent is not enough — the model must also be told when to search, and the search itself must return distilled highlights rather than whole pages. The episode is mostly a product-and-architecture talk about semantic search for coding and review agents; the title's "six months out of date" framing is the hook for the first few minutes, after which the discussion moves to token efficiency, transparency, provider neutrality, and Exa's newer Agent offering. Hojsan's core claim is that coding agents do not need "10 blue links." Exa returns context-rich highlights — by his account, roughly 500 characters instead of 100,000 — computed at runtime without an LLM, so no extra latency is added to the search call. He names Cursor, Cognition, Warp, and CodeRabbit as companies using Exa to power web search, and describes a two-step integration pattern: instruct the agent when to search, then execute the search. The briefing below covers the knowledge-cutoff problem, the highlight mechanism, the transparency and cost case against native search tools, the multi-provider argument, the Exa Agent launch with its data partners, and the re-ranking and schema-generation details from the Q&A. ## The knowledge cutoff leaves a review gap no model release closes Hojsan's central problem statement is that every LLM has a knowledge cutoff, and the lag between cutoff date and model release date runs around six months. Anything merged into a repository inside that window is invisible to the model — not just un-creatable as net-new code, but unreviewable. He uses a concrete example: a PR to the Kuder vector store made a few months before the talk, which falls inside the blind spot after GPT-5.5's cutoff date. His contrast is between how a human and a model handle the same diff. A human would go to Stack Overflow, ask whether a variable — in his example, one called "inertia check" — was removed, paste the compile error, get an answer, and open a PR. A model without web search looks at the same diff and concludes it is a cleanup. Hojsan says that reading is wrong: the parameter is being removed because the change is actually a dependency bump requiring a refactor. With web search, the agent can pull the repository itself and any breaking changes from the changelog, then explain the migration in depth. > "Many people without web search will go see, OK, here's the error. Broadcom is a custom chip and networking leader. If you have $1,000 that you're ready to invest today, that would be enough to start positions in two of the chip stocks that look poised to lead the next wave of the artificial intelligence (AI) build-out in **Advanced Micro Devices**(NASDAQ: AMD) and **Broadcom**(NASDAQ: AVGO). With $1,000, you could buy one share of each. Let's look at why these two [semiconductor stocks](https://www.fool.com/investing/stock-market/market-sectors/information-technology/semiconductor-stocks/?utm_source=globeandmail&utm_medium=feed&utm_campaign=article&referring_guid=93094985-7367-4b97-869d-45c8768513a9) look like solid investments. ***Missed Nvidia in 2009? This Rare Signal Is Flashing Again.**In 2009, a "Double Down" signal flashed for a little-known chipmaker called Nvidia. For the first time in years, that same "Total Conviction" signal is flashing for a company 1/100th the size of Nvidia. [**Continue »**](https://api.fool.com/infotron/infotrack/click?apikey=35527423-a535-4519-a07f-20014582e03e&impression=619bbc8f-82c0-4fbd-b781-56e2e798d533&url=https%3A%2F%2Fwww.fool.com%2Fmms%2Fmark%2Fa-sa-dd-total-conviction%3Faid%3D11123%26source%3Disaediica0000078%26ftm_cam%3Dsa-dd-4%26ftm_veh%3Dtop_incontent_pitch_feed_partner%26ftm_pit%3D19478&utm_source=globeandmail&utm_medium=feed&utm_campaign=article&referring_guid=93094985-7367-4b97-869d-45c8768513a9)* ## 1. AMD: An inference, agentic AI, and physical AI winner AMD was outmaneuvered by **Nvidia** in the AI training market, but it's positioning itself to prevent that from happening again. It's developing processors that target the inference, agentic AI, and physical AI markets, and aims to be a viable contender in all three. It has also been making significant investments in memory. This positions it well for the inference market, where architectures that prioritize high volumes of fast memory access are favored over raw compute power. The chiplet design of its graphics processing units (GPUs) allows them to be packaged with more memory, and AMD has also formed a partnership with **Cerebras** to offer a disaggregated inference solution that combines both of their systems. It has also inked a deal to acquire inference chipmaker Taalas, which hardwires AI models directly into its chips. It also bought memory optimization company MEXT earlier this year. And AMD has two $100 billion inference deals in place with OpenAI and **Meta Platforms**, as well as a large agreement with Anthropic. On top of that, the company is a leader in the data center central processing unit (CPU) market. This market has been exploding with the rise of agentic AI, as servers dedicated to powering AI agents require considerably more CPUs than those used for AI training. AMD forecasts that the data center CPU market will grow to $220 billion in the coming years, although in light of the rapidly growing popularity of Meta's new Muse agentic AI offering, this estimate could prove low. Meta, by the way, is running its Muse agents on AMD's CPUs. Finally, with its agreement to acquire AI model and research lab World Labs, AMD is improving its ability to pursue the physical AI and robotics markets. World Lab's expertise lies in spatial intelligence models, and it will provide AMD with the tools to advance an open AI ecosystem (in contrast to Nvidia's closed system) that serves those emerging AI markets. This deal isn't about selling more chips in the near term, but rather about creating future architectures and platforms for physical AI. Given all its opportunities for growth ahead, AMD stock is a buy. ![AMD and Broadcom logos.](https://barchart-news-media-prod.aws.barchart.com/FC/e0d2edd172dd97f7acbf3942...

Infra & Chips.content: ![]() ![GuruFocus](https://s3.tradingview.com/news/logo/gurufocus--theme-light.svg) ![GuruFocus](https://s3.tradingview.com/news/logo/gurufocus--theme-dark.svg) # Broadcom Is Lining Up $60 Billion to Fuel the AI Chip Race Against Nvidia ![](https://s3-symbol-logo.tradingview.com/broadcom.svg) Broadcom Inc. (AVGO, Financials), the chip and infrastructure software company, could get another boost from the artificial intelligence spending boom as Wall Street works to assemble $60 billion in financing for chips and data-center equipment used by Anthropic and other AI companies. The size of the package is notable even by the standards of the current AI buildout. Banks are preparing to syndicate $42 billion of senior-secured debt, according to the report. Blackstone is leading another $18 billion of junior debt and plans to provide $9 billion from its own funds before syndicating the rest. For Broadcom, the financing could help turn demand for AI computing into additional chip and equipment sales. The company has been expanding its position in AI infrastructure, putting it in more direct competition with Nvidia for a growing pool of data-center spending. But there is another side to the story. Building AI infrastructure increasingly depends on enormous amounts of outside capital. That makes lenders' willingness to fund these projects almost as important as demand for the technology itself. The $60 billion package therefore offers investors a useful test of both Broadcom's AI opportunity and Wall Street's appetite for financing it. The next thing to watch is whether the debt package attracts enough demand to move forward as planned. ## [AVGO chart](/chart/?symbol=NASDAQ%3AAVGO) ## [Latest news](/news-flow) ## [More news from GuruFocus](/news-flow/?provider=gurufocus) Select market data provided by [ICE Data Services](https://www.ice.com/fixed-income-data-services).
